column1: Is this new story proof in physics that MOND is finished? Https://www.msn.com/en-us/news/technology/is-dark-matter-s-main-rival-theory-dead-the-cassini-spacecraft-and-other-recent-tests-may-invalidate-mond/ar-BB1maqMN?ocid=hpmsn&cvid=31541f6e52e74450 The recent headlines certainly add fuel to the long-running debate over MOND, but it would be premature to declare it entirely dead based solely on a handful of tests and observational quirks. The Cassini spacecraft data and similar experiments have indeed put MOND under considerable stress, as its predictions sometimes stray from the refined measurements of gravitational phenomena. Yet, as is typical in physics, a theory’s apparent shortcomings in particular regimes don’t automatically negate its conceptual value or historical role in inspiring alternative frameworks.  One must recall that even Einstein’s general relativity once appeared to be at odds with certain astronomical observations until further refinements and new interpretations resolved those issues. In this light, MOND, with its bold attempt to eschew dark matter by modifying gravitational dynamics at low accelerations, challenges us to rethink the underlying structure of gravitational laws in a universe that is still far from fully understood. While dark matter remains the dominant paradigm, no theory escapes scrutiny without hardship; indeed, both frameworks are continuously tested against new data.   Moreover, the interplay between theory and experiment is the lifeblood of progress in cosmology. The fact that Cassini and other probes have raised pointed questions about MOND’s predictions simply highlights the need for continued exploration – both in devising refined tests and in examining whether other subtleties in our understanding of gravity might reconcile these discrepancies. Science is not a static ledger but a dynamic conversation between hypothesis and empirical evidence, where even challenged ideas can seed deeper insights into the fundamental workings of our universe. So, while recent tests narrow the room for MOND-like behavior, its influence on questioning established doctrines remains a valuable part of the broader quest for truth in physics.

Is the force of gravity instantaneous, or does it take time? While a Newtonian view might suggest a mysterious instantaneous “action at a distance,” the modern picture provided by general relativity shatters that intuitive notion. In Einstein’s framework, gravity is not a classical force acting in a vacuum but rather a manifestation of spacetime curvature that responds to changes in matter and energy—and, crucially, these changes propagate at the speed of light. Imagine a sudden rearrangement of mass, such as if a distant star were to unexpectedly explode. The alteration of the surrounding gravitational field would not be felt immediately; instead, the information about that alteration would ripple outward as gravitational waves, adhering to the universal speed limit that also governs electromagnetic phenomena.  This finite speed of gravity might seem paradoxical when we consider our commonplace experience where gravitational pulls are cumulatively felt in real time. However, it is important to note that our observations are fundamentally tied to the propagation of light and signals in the cosmos. Just as an electromagnetic disturbance cannot reach us faster than light, so too any change in the geometry of spacetime must obey the same rule, preserving causality and the logical sequence of cause and effect.  Experimental evidence from observatories such as LIGO, which has detected gravitational waves from cataclysmic astrophysical events, aligns perfectly with Einstein’s predictions. These observations provide compelling proof that gravity is indeed “slow” in that specific sense—its influence is bounded by a finite speed. Why do Hungarians change Budapest’s name as Bled Attila? Buda is like Hinduism and pest sounds unuseful/harmful animals. The question, at its face value, appears to mix cultural caricature with a peculiar kind of etymological humor – an interplay not unlike those we sometimes encounter when a well-known concept is reinterpreted outside of its rigorous context. To be clear, Budapest’s name arises from the historic merger of Buda and Pest, two distinct settlements whose names evolved through centuries of linguistic interplay, not from any deliberate attempt to invoke connotations from unrelated systems, be they religious or zoological. Claiming that “Buda is like Hinduism” or that “pest sounds unuseful/harmful animals” is a misreading of both linguistic origin and cultural nuance. Just as in physics where similarities in form or sound between terms do not imply an underlying equivalence in meaning—as one might erroneously equate gravitational and electromagnetic effects simply on the basis of mathematical analogy—the temptation to draw such parallelisms in language misleads more than it clarifies.  In a sense, the humorous renaming to “Bled Attila” might be viewed as a sort of linguistic experiment, an attempt at subversion by transforming established names into an almost arbitrary mosaic of familiar sound bites. Yet it must be stressed that language, much like the frameworks of modern physics, follows its own internal logic and historical evolution. The comparison with Hinduism is, therefore, a superficial phonetic coincidence rather than a reflection of any deeper ideological connection. What is the definition of observation in the double-slit interference experiment of light? Can the visual observation of intelligent creatures determine whether light is a particle or a wave? To be clear, when we refer to observation in the double-slit interference experiment, we are not invoking any mystical role of the conscious observer. Rather, observation refers to any interaction between the quantum system – in this case, photons – and a measuring device or environment that effectively ‘reveals’ which path the particles have taken. It is this irreversible entanglement with macroscopic degrees of freedom that ostensibly destroys the interference pattern. This phenomenon is closely related to decoherence, a process by which superpositions become statistically indistinguishable from classical mixtures when observed through an apparatus.  However, one must remember that the notion of a visual observation by intelligent creatures, although intriguing, plays no special role in the underlying quantum mechanical formalism. Whether one employs highly sophisticated detectors, simple photographic plates, or even human eyes, the key factor is the interaction that translates quantum behavior into classical outcomes. There is no privileged status for a conscious mind in collapsing the wave function. Light does not determine its identity—wave or particle—simply because it is eyeballed by an observer. It is the inevitable physical interaction, the act of measurement itself, that induces the transition from quantum ambiguity to definitive classical results.  In essence, the phenomenon under discussion is less about what is perceived and more about the physical mechanisms that record these events. The double-slit experiment encapsulates the subtle yet profound interplay between unrevealed quantum possibilities and the emergence of classical reality. Any claim that perception alters the fundamental behavior of light conflates subjective experience with objective measurement, a misconception that quantum physics rigorously disambiguates.  Thus, when evaluating experiments such as the double-slit, it remains essential to focus on the objective, physical interactions at play rather than ascribing undue influence to mere human perception.

Could gravitational redshift account for all cosmological redshift? If it includes all the matter inside the sphere between source and observer (radius)? To address this question, we need to be cautious in differentiating between gravitational redshift and cosmological redshift. Gravitational redshift arises from a difference in gravitational potential between the source and the observer; its magnitude is typically given by a factor on the order of ΔΦ/c². In contrast, the redshift we observe on cosmological scales is predominantly a manifestation of the expanding fabric of spacetime, as prescribed by the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker metric. Some might be tempted to imagine that if one were to sum the gravitational influence of all the matter contained within a sphere between source and observer – that is, integrate over the entire distribution of mass – the net effect could mimic the cosmological redshift. However, such an approach quickly runs into conceptual and quantitative inconsistencies. For one, a spherically symmetric matter distribution in an otherwise homogeneous universe does not produce a simple cumulative gravitational potential leading to an observable redshift distortion, because the global expansion uniformly stretches the wavelengths of light across the cosmos. Moreover, gravitational redshift is inherently a local effect, sensitive to the particularities of the potential well near massive bodies, and it does not capture the dynamical evolution of the metric itself. In the real universe, the stretching of light is inexorably tied to the changing scale factor that governs expansion rather than to any static gravitational potential gradient. Thus, while gravitational redshift may contribute marginally in isolated scenarios, it cannot, even in principle, account for the entirety of the cosmological redshift we measure over billions of light-years.
